notes.meaning: The five kings were brought out from the dark cave where they had taken refuge. Listing each king by name highlighted how great the victory was over their entire coalition. Their secret hiding spot could not save them once God set the time for judgment.

Joshua called his army commanders forward and told them to step on the necks of the defeated kings. In the ancient world, this was a well-known sign showing that an enemy was completely subdued. It was a sign to reassure Israel's leaders that the Lord would bring all their proud foes under their feet.

Joshua urged his men to be strong and courageous rather than fearful. He used the very same words God had given him when their journey first began. Seeing these five rulers brought low proved that the Lord would do the exact same thing to every enemy they fought.

Joshua put the five kings to death and hung their bodies on trees until the evening. Hanging a body after execution was a public sign of shame to warn other enemies not to resist God. Joshua followed God's law by displaying them only during daylight hours.

At sunset, Joshua ordered the bodies taken down and thrown back into the very cave where they had hidden. Large stones were placed over the opening, turning their intended shelter into a sealed tomb. Those stones remained as a lasting marker of God's justice against rebellion.

Joshua captured the city of Makkedah on that same day, striking down its king and its inhabitants. The city was devoted to destruction, meaning it was completely set apart for God's judgment and nothing was spared. Joshua dealt with Makkedah's king just as he had dealt with the king of Jericho.

Joshua and his army marched from Makkedah to attack Libnah. The Lord handed the city over, and the Israelites put everyone inside to the sword, leaving no survivors. Its king received the same judgment as the king of Jericho, showing that no royal city could resist God's decree.

The army next moved against Lachish, which was a heavily fortified city in the foothills. Lachish held out against the initial assault, but Joshua captured it on the second day. Its fall proved that even strong defenses could not protect a city once the Lord gave it into Israel's hands.

King Horam of Gezer marched out with his army to come to the aid of Lachish. Joshua met this new threat and wiped out Horam and his troops before they could save the city. Trying to help those who fought against God only brought swift ruin upon Gezer's forces.

Joshua advanced from Lachish to the city of Eglon with the entire army. They surrounded it and captured it on that very first day, executing God's sentence of judgment against everyone in it. The swift fall of Eglon matched the fate of the cities that fell before it.

The army marched up from the lowlands into the mountains to attack the city of Hebron. Joshua captured the city, its dependent towns, and its new king, who had taken power after the first king died at Makkedah. The Israelites carried out God's judgment thoroughly across the whole district.

Joshua then turned his forces toward Debir and fought against it. Israel captured the city, its king, and all the nearby villages under its control, leaving no survivors. Joshua followed the exact same pattern of complete obedience that he had shown at Hebron and Libnah.

Joshua conquered the entire southern region, covering the hill country, the Negev desert, the foothills, and the slopes. He devoted to destruction everything that breathed, exactly as the Lord had commanded. This sweeping judgment cleared out the corrupt Canaanite rule so Israel could later settle the land.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars view the phrase about destroying everything that breathed as common ancient military rhetoric for total victory, noting that later chapters describe Canaanites still living in these same areas.

notes.meaning: The campaign swept from Kadesh-barnea in the far south over to Gaza on the coastal plain, and across the district of Goshen up to Gibeon. This Goshen was a town and territory in southern Judah, not the land in Egypt. These boundaries defined the full territory secured during Joshua's southern sweep.

Joshua took all these kings and their lands in a single campaign. The writer gives all credit to God, stating plainly that this quick success happened because the Lord fought for Israel. True victory always belongs to God rather than human military strength.

After subduing the southern kings and their strongholds, Joshua led the entire army back to the camp at Gilgal. There the nation could regroup, give thanks to God, and prepare for their next steps. Gilgal served as their spiritual home base throughout the conquest.
